## Salesforce vs Follow Up Boss for Real Estate
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-salesforce-vs-follow-up-boss-real-estate.html

Salesforce vs Follow Up Boss for Real Estate: Which CRM Is Right for You?
Two CRMs dominate the real estate conversation: Follow Up Boss — purpose-built for residential real estate teams — and Salesforce — the world's most powerful CRM platform. Both can run a real estate business. They're built for very different ones.
This comparison is written from the perspective of someone who has configured Salesforce for real estate companies. It's not a sales pitch for either platform — it's an honest breakdown of when each one wins.
Category | Follow Up Boss | Salesforce
Setup complexity | Low — ready in hours | High — needs proper configuration
Real estate-specific features | Built-in (MLS sync, lead routing) | Requires configuration or AppExchange
Automation depth | Good for basic workflows | Unlimited with Flow Builder
Reporting & dashboards | Standard reports | Advanced with Tableau integration
Customization | Limited to platform | Fully customizable objects & fields
Scalability | Good for <50 agents | Enterprise-grade, unlimited scale
Cost (per seat) | Lower ($69–$500/mo flat) | Higher ($150+ per user/mo)
Integration ecosystem | Real estate focused | 5,000+ integrations via AppExchange
AI and predictive tools | Basic | Einstein AI, predictive scoring
Support for multiple business lines | Residential only | Any property type or vertical
When Follow Up Boss Wins
Follow Up Boss is the right choice if you run a residential real estate team of under 20-30 agents and your primary workflow is lead follow-up, showing scheduling, and simple pipeline management. It's genuinely easier to set up, the MLS integrations work out of the box, and your agents will adopt it faster because it's built specifically for how residential agents think.
If your business model is straightforward — inbound leads, agent follow-up, transactions — Follow Up Boss does this well at a lower cost and lower friction.
When Salesforce Wins
Salesforce becomes the clear winner the moment your real estate business gets complex. This includes any of the following:
Property acquisition companies — tracking properties through multi-stage acquisition, renovation, and sale pipelines that Follow Up Boss can't model
Real estate investment firms — needing ROI tracking, investor reporting, and multi-portfolio dashboards
Brokerages with 30+ agents — needing sophisticated territory management, performance analytics, and commission tracking
Companies with multiple business lines — combining residential, commercial, and property management in one CRM
Teams that need deep integrations — connecting CRM to accounting systems, custom databases, or proprietary tools
The companies I work with moved to Salesforce specifically because they outgrew their previous CRM — often Follow Up Boss or similar tools — and needed reporting, automation, and integration capabilities that simpler platforms can't provide.
The Honest Answer: It Depends on Where You're Going
If you're running a small residential team today and don't plan to grow significantly, Follow Up Boss is probably the right call. Salesforce's power comes with complexity, and complexity has a cost — in configuration time, in training, and in ongoing administration.
If you're building toward scale — more agents, more properties, more data, more business lines — Salesforce is worth the investment. A well-configured Salesforce setup grows with you indefinitely. You'll never outgrow it.
The question isn't which CRM is better. It's which one fits where your business is going.

## Connect Your Real Estate Stack to Salesforce with Zapier
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-zapier-salesforce-real-estate.html

Connecting Salesforce to Your Real Estate Stack with Zapier
The average real estate company uses 8-12 software tools. Their CRM is one of them. And most of the time, none of these tools talk to each other — which means data gets manually copied between systems, leads get lost in transitions, and nobody has a complete picture. Zapier is the connective tissue that makes Salesforce the center of your entire operation without writing a single line of code.
The 5 Integrations That Deliver the Most Value
1. Website Forms to Salesforce Lead
Every form submission on your website should instantly create a Lead in Salesforce — not batched overnight, not manually entered from an inbox, but instantly, with all form fields mapped and assignment rules triggered. Build this first. It closes the biggest data gap in most real estate organizations and takes about 20 minutes to configure in Zapier.
2. Zillow and Realtor.com to Salesforce Lead
These platforms email lead notifications. Zapier watches the inbox, parses lead details from the email, and creates a Salesforce Lead record automatically. Combined with assignment rules, the lead reaches an agent before anyone has even opened the email notification.
At Central City Solutions, this kind of integration puts every new lead in front of a rep within minutes instead of waiting in an inbox.
3. Facebook Lead Ads to Salesforce
Facebook Lead Ads is one of the most effective lead generation tools for real estate — and one of the least connected to CRMs. Zapier has a native Facebook Lead Ads trigger that fires the moment someone submits a form, creating an instant Salesforce record with full campaign attribution.
4. Closed Deal to Finance System
When an opportunity is marked Closed Won, Zapier automatically updates your financial tracking spreadsheet, notifies the transaction team, and creates a record in your commission calculation system. Zero manual handoff between CRM and finance.
5. Stale Lead Alert to Slack
Combined with a Salesforce Flow flagging leads with no activity in 72 hours, Zapier posts an automatic Slack message to the relevant channel with the lead name, assigned agent, and days since last contact. This makes the invisible visible in real time — without anyone having to run a report.
Zapier is great until it isn’t — at Central City Solutions we eventually moved 30+ Zaps to native Flows. Start simple, plan the graduation path. See the full case study →
Zapier vs Native Salesforce Integrations
When a well-maintained native AppExchange integration exists for a tool you use, prefer it over Zapier — native integrations tend to be more reliable with tighter field mapping. Use Zapier for everything that lacks a quality native connector, or where the native connector is missing specific functionality you need.
Building Your Integration Map
Before touching Zapier, document every tool your team uses and every data flow between them. Identify which flows are currently manual. Start with the one that involves the most manual work or the longest delays — that is your highest-value first integration.

## BRRRR Calculator: Cash Left In, Cash Flow & ROI (Free)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/brrrr-calculator.html

BRRRR calculator.
Buy, rehab, rent, refinance, repeat. Enter the purchase, rehab and refinance terms to see how much of your cash stays in the deal, the new loan payment, monthly cash flow and your cash-on-cash return. Built for real estate investors in the United States, Canada, the UK and Europe. Pick your currency; the math is the same everywhere.
The formula
Total project cost = purchase + rehab + closing + holding + refinance costs
New loan = ARV × refinance LTV
Cash left in the deal = total project cost − new loan
Monthly cash flow = rent − operating costs − new loan payment
Cash-on-cash return = (monthly cash flow × 12) ÷ cash left in the deal
Worked example
Buy at $120,000, spend $35,000 on rehab, $3,000 closing and $4,000 holding. The house appraises at $210,000 and the lender refinances at 75%: a $157,500 loan. With $4,000 of refinance costs, the whole project costs $166,000, so $8,500 of your cash stays in. At 7.5% over 30 years the payment is $1,101 a month. Rent of $1,850 minus $550 of costs and the payment leaves $199 a month, a 28.1% cash-on-cash return.
Questions
What is the BRRRR method?
BRRRR stands for buy, rehab, rent, refinance, repeat. You buy a property below its after-repair value, renovate it, rent it out, then refinance at the new appraised value to pull your cash back out and use it on the next deal.
What does "cash left in the deal" mean?
It is the money you still have tied up after the refinance: everything you spent to buy, fix, hold and refinance the property, minus the new loan. A perfect BRRRR leaves zero or less, which means the refinance paid you back in full.
What loan-to-value do lenders use for a BRRRR refinance?
For investment properties, cash-out refinance lenders commonly lend around 70% to 80% of the appraised value. In Canada, conventional rental refinances are often capped at 80%. Check current terms with your lender, since they change with the market.
Is there a waiting period before refinancing?
Many lenders apply a seasoning period, often around six months of ownership, before they lend on the new appraised value instead of the purchase price. Some DSCR and portfolio lenders are more flexible. Confirm with your lender before you buy.
How do I track BRRRR deals across a portfolio?
Keep purchase, rehab, appraisal, refinance and rent figures as fields on each property record in your CRM, with cash left in and cash-on-cash as formulas. Then a portfolio report shows which deals recycled your capital and which did not.
Related free tools
Rental yield & cap rate calculator · DSCR calculator · MAO calculator · All free tools
Last updated October 2026. For planning only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Check figures with your lender, accountant or lawyer.
Add this calculator to your site
Free to embed on your blog or investor site. Copy the code below.

## Cash Buyers List Template for Wholesalers (Free CSV)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/cash-buyers-list-template.html

Cash buyers list template for wholesalers.
A cash buyers list works when every buyer's buy box is saved as fields, not buried in texts and DMs. Then each new deal goes to the 10 buyers who fit its area, price, property type and rehab level, instead of a blast to everyone. Download the free template below and fill it once per buyer.
Download the CSV template Opens in Google Sheets, Excel or any CRM import.
The fields to capture
How to send each deal to the right buyers
1. Filter: area matches, price between min and max, property type matches, rehab level matches
2. Drop buyers who need vacant if the property is occupied
3. Sort: last bought date (newest first), then reply rate
4. Send to the top 10 first; widen only if nobody bites
5. Log every send and every reply on the buyer
Logging the sends and replies is what turns a list into data. After a few months you can see which buyers actually close, which sources produce them, and which deals got no interest because the price or area was wrong.
Check the deal works for the buyer first
A deal that leaves the buyer no margin sits no matter how good your list is. Run it through the free wholesale deal analyzer to see the buyer's all-in cost and profit after your fee before you send it.
Questions
What is a cash buyers list?
A list of investors who buy properties, usually for cash or with short-term financing, that a wholesaler sends deals to. It is only useful if each buyer's buy box is saved as fields, so every deal goes to the buyers who actually fit.
How many buyers do I need?
Fewer than most people think, if they are the right ones. Ten active buyers who match your areas and price range and have bought recently are worth more than a thousand names that never reply.
Where do cash buyers come from?
Common sources are public records of recent cash purchases, title companies and closing attorneys who work with investors, local real estate investor association meetings, landlords in your target areas, and buyers who reply to your deal posts. Record the source on each buyer.
How do I keep the list clean?
Merge duplicates by phone and email, ask for fresh proof of funds when the date gets old, and move buyers who never reply after several matching deals off the main list instead of deleting them.
Can I use this in a CRM?
Yes. Each column becomes a field on a contact or buyer record. The free CRM field kit has the same buyer fields with picklist values and automation rules for Salesforce, REsimpli, Podio, HubSpot or a spreadsheet.

## Cold Caller to Acquisitions Handoff: Fields & Rules
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/cold-caller-handoff-checklist.html

Cold caller to acquisitions handoff: the fields and rules.
Most cold calling teams lose deals at the handoff, not on the call. The caller marks a lead "warm", acquisitions calls back with no context, and the seller has to start over. Fix it with three things: a short fixed list of call outcomes, fields that must be filled before a lead can be passed, and a callback time rule your CRM enforces.
1. A fixed list of call outcomes
Not interested · Wrong number · Call back later · Warm · Hot
Five options, picked from a list, never typed. Free text makes reporting impossible.
2. Required before a lead is passed
Field | Warm | Hot | Why
Timeline to sell | Required | Required | Sets the follow-up cadence
Reason for selling | Required | Required | The first thing acquisitions needs to hear
Property condition | Required | Required | Feeds the repair estimate and MAO
Asking price (if given) | Optional | Required | Shows the gap to your offer early
Decision makers on title | Optional | Required | Avoids appointments with the wrong person
Best callback time | Required | Required | Gets the second call answered
3. A callback time rule
Set a rule and let the CRM enforce it
Hot leads alert the acquisitions manager and get a callback task due within the hour. Warm leads get a task due the same day. Any task past due shows up on a daily "late callbacks" list. Pick times that fit your team, then make the CRM create the tasks so nobody has to remember.
4. A 20-minute weekly check
1. Pull last week's Warm and Hot leads by caller
2. Compare each caller's outcome with what acquisitions found on the callback
3. Count missing required fields per caller
4. Coach the caller with the biggest gap, one thing at a time
Investors on BiggerPockets debate lead managers vs acquisitions managers and VAs for cold calling ; whichever setup you choose, the handoff rules above stay the same.
Questions
What should a cold caller collect before passing a lead?
At minimum: timeline to sell, reason for selling, property condition and best callback time. For hot leads add asking price and who is on title.
How fast should acquisitions call back a hot lead?
Set a rule your team can keep, such as within the hour for hot and the same day for warm, and have the CRM create the task and flag it when it is late.
How do I check if my VAs are qualifying leads correctly?
Once a week, compare each caller's Warm and Hot leads with what acquisitions found on the callback, and count missing required fields per caller.
Can a CRM block incomplete handoffs?
Yes. Most CRMs, including Salesforce, can require fields before a status changes, so a lead cannot be marked Hot until the key questions are answered.

## Free Wholesaling CRM Field Kit: Fields, Picklists, Rules
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/crm-field-kit.html

The wholesaling CRM field kit.
The fields, picklists, automation rules and Monday report that keep deals from leaking between the marketing dollar and the closed deal. Copy them into Salesforce, REsimpli, Podio, HubSpot or a spreadsheet. Free to use and change.
1. Lead fields (13)
Where each lead came from, what happens next and how fast you reached the seller. The two that matter most: Lead Source required before a lead leaves New, and Next Task Date required on every open lead.
Field name | Type | Required when | Why it matters
Lead Source | Picklist | Before Status can leave New | Without it, no report can tie a contract or a closed deal back to the channel that paid for it.
Campaign | Lookup to Campaign (or text) | Before Status can leave New, when Lead Source is a paid channel | Lead Source says which channel; Campaign says which mailer, list or ad. Spend is entered on the campaign, so cost per appointment and ROI need this link.
Market | Picklist | Always | Lets you compare channels and reps market by market instead of mixing a strong market with a weak one.
Status | Picklist | Always | One shared list of stages, so a report can count how many leads sit at each step and how long they stay there.
Next Task Date | Date | While the lead is open (Status is not Dead or Under Contract) | An open lead with no next date is a lead nobody is working. This field makes the gap visible and lets you block it.
Touch Count | Number (auto) | Never entered by hand; counted from logged calls, texts and emails to the seller | Shows how much follow-up a lead actually got before it was marked Dead or went under contract.
Video: Leads with no next step → Video: Missed seller calls →
2. Deal fields (23)
Underwriting on the deal itself: MAO as a formula, your repair estimate next to the buyer's, and booked fees kept separate from the fees you actually receive.
Field name | Type | Required when | Why it matters
Lead Source | Picklist (copied from lead, locked) | Copied when the deal is created; not editable after | Keeps attribution intact from first call to closing so contracts and fees count for the right channel.
Campaign | Lookup to Campaign (copied from lead, locked) | Copied when the deal is created; not editable after | Contracts per campaign and ROI by campaign both read this field.
Deal Status | Picklist | Always | Separates deals that are booked from deals that are actually kept.
ARV | Currency | Before Deal Status can move to Offer Sent | After-repair value from comps. Everything in MAO starts here.
Your Repair Estimate | Currency | Before Deal Status can move to Offer Sent | Your team's repair number, the one MAO uses.
Buyer's Repair Estimate | Currency | When a buyer walks the property (optional) | What the end buyer thinks repairs cost. Comparing it with yours shows whether your estimates run low.
Video: Offers off-formula → MAO calculator →
3. Buyer fields (10)
Turn the buyer list into a database, so each deal goes to the buyers who actually buy that kind of house first.
Field name | Type | Required when | Why it matters
Zips | Long text (comma-separated) or multi-select | Before the buyer gets deal blasts | Lets you send each deal only to buyers who buy in that zip.
Max Price | Currency | Before the buyer gets deal blasts | Filters out buyers who can't pay your price, so the list stays short and relevant.
Rehab Level | Multi-select picklist | Before the buyer gets deal blasts | A buyer who only wants light rehabs ignores a full gut, and the reverse.
Closing Speed (days) | Number | Optional | When an inspection period is short, you want the buyers who actually close fast.
Last Bought Date | Date | Updated when the buyer closes one of your deals (or from public records) | Separates active buyers from names on a list.
Using a spreadsheet for buyers? Start from the free cash buyers list template (CSV).
Wholesaling CRM glossary →
4. Automation rules (10)
Plain-English rules that keep the fields filled in and honest, each with a Salesforce hint and an any-CRM hint.
No lead leaves New without a source
Every logged touch counts, and the first one is stamped
A missed seller call becomes a callback task in 5 minutes
No open lead without a next date
Dead needs a reason
Dead Reason sets the revisit date
Offers above MAO need a second pair of eyes
Signing a contract stamps the numbers that matter later
A fall-out zeroes the fee and records why
Every Monday, list the hot leads nobody touched
5. Monday report spec
The five numbers to look at every Monday and the exact fields each one reads from.
Cost per appointment, by campaign
Contracts per campaign
Contract to first seller call
Booked revenue, forecast vs. actual
ROI that counts the deals you keep
The Monday 5 → The Kept-Deal Map →
Questions
Is it really free? Do I need to give my email?
Yes, it's free and there's no form. Download the files, copy them, change them. Credit is nice but not required.
Does it only work in Salesforce?
No. Every field and rule has a plain-English version for any CRM, including REsimpli, Podio, HubSpot or a spreadsheet. Where Salesforce needs something specific, there's a one-line Salesforce hint.
Where should I start if I can only do one thing?
Make Lead Source required before a lead leaves New, and make Next Task Date required on every open lead. Those two fields fix the most common leaks: not knowing which marketing pays, and leads nobody follows up.
Why these fields and not others?
Each one exists so a specific weekly number can be counted: cost per appointment by campaign, contracts per campaign, time from contract to first seller call, booked versus closed revenue, and ROI on kept deals.

## Do I Need a CRM Yet? Spreadsheet vs CRM for Wholesalers
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/do-i-need-a-crm-wholesaling.html

Do I need a CRM yet? Spreadsheet vs CRM for wholesalers.
You need a CRM when a lead can be forgotten without anyone noticing. Deal count matters less than people, follow-up and lead source. If one person works every lead and checks the sheet daily, a spreadsheet can carry you. Once two people touch leads, follow-ups run past a week, or you can't say which list paid for your last deal, the sheet starts costing you deals.
Seven signs you've outgrown the spreadsheet
Check the ones that are true
☐ More than one person calls or texts sellers ☐ Follow-ups depend on someone remembering ☐ You can't say which list or campaign produced your last closed deal ☐ A missed call doesn't turn into a callback task by itself ☐ Leads with "not right now" have no next date ☐ Your buyers list is a text thread or a column of phone numbers ☐ Monday numbers take an hour to rebuild by hand
Two or more checked: the spreadsheet is already costing you. Wholesalers describe it the same way on BiggerPockets: "leads die in the follow-up" .
What a spreadsheet still does well
Keep it if
You're solo, every lead is touched daily, and you're still testing which marketing works. A sheet with lead source, status, next follow-up date and notes is a fine start. Make next follow-up date a column you sort by every morning.
The cheapest next step
1. Write your stages from new lead to closed on one page
2. Make lead source, next follow-up date and status required on every lead
3. Move the sheet into a free or low-cost CRM trial and test it for 2 weeks
4. Turn on two automations: missed call = callback task, no next date = alert
5. Only then compare paid tools against the flow you wrote in step 1
Looking at low-cost options? A recent BiggerPockets thread compares them: low to no cost wholesaling CRMs . Whatever you pick, check it against the wholesaling CRM checklist .
Questions
How many leads before I need a CRM?
There is no single number. The trigger is people and follow-up: once two people touch leads, or follow-ups depend on memory, a CRM pays for itself by keeping leads from going quiet.
Can I use Google Sheets as a CRM?
Yes at the start, if one person works every lead daily and the sheet has lead source, status, next follow-up date and notes. It breaks when you add people, texting and automated reminders.
What should I set up first in a new CRM?
Required lead source, a next follow-up date on every open lead, a missed call creating a callback task, and a short list of stages. Fancy dashboards can wait.
Is Salesforce too much for a new wholesaler?
Usually yes. Start with a spreadsheet or an investor CRM. Salesforce makes sense once you have several people, markets or reporting needs your tool cannot handle.

## Double Closing Costs for Wholesalers: Both Sides, One Formula
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/double-closing-costs.html

Double closing costs: both sides, one formula.
In a double close you buy the property from the seller and resell it to your end buyer, usually the same day. You pay buyer-side costs on the first closing and seller-side costs on the second, plus transactional funding if you borrow the purchase money. What you keep is the resale price minus your contract price minus all of that.
The formula
Closing A (you buy) = settlement fee + title insurance and recording you pay + any transfer tax your side pays
Closing B (you sell) = settlement fee + transfer tax, deed prep and any title costs your side pays
Funding = transactional funding fee, if you do not use your own cash
You keep = resale price − contract price − Closing A − Closing B − Funding
Which side pays transfer tax and owner's title insurance depends on the state, county and contract. Ask your title company for a settlement estimate for each closing and put every line in one of the two buckets above.
Double close or assignment?
An assignment has one closing, and your fee is paid at it. A double close keeps your spread off the assignment paperwork, and works when the contract can't be assigned, but costs a second closing and often funding. Put your numbers into the free assignment vs double close calculator to see what you keep each way. If the assignment fee would be large enough to put the buyer off, also check that the deal still works for them in the wholesale deal analyzer .
Ask your title company before you sign
1. Do you close back-to-back transactions?
Some title companies don't. Find one that does before you go under contract.
2. What will each closing cost?
A settlement estimate for closing A and closing B, line by line, at your contract and resale prices.
3. Will the end buyer's lender accept it?
If your buyer is financing, some lenders have rules about how recently the seller took title. Cash buyers avoid this.
4. Can transactional funding be used here?
Confirm the title company works with your funder and when the funds must arrive.
What to track in your CRM
Exit type and both sets of costs
A picklist for assignment or double close on every deal, with closing A, closing B and funding costs as fields. Reports by exit type then show what you actually kept, not just the spread.
Questions
What is a double close?
Two closings back to back, often the same day. In the first you buy the property from the seller; in the second you sell it to your end buyer. You are the buyer in one and the seller in the other, so you pay closing costs on both.
Why double close instead of assigning?
Usually because the spread is large and you do not want the seller or buyer to see it on the assignment paperwork, or because the contract does not allow assignment. The cost is a second set of closing costs and, if you do not use your own cash, transactional funding.
How much does a double close cost?
It depends on the state, county, title company and price, so there is no single number. Ask your title company for a settlement estimate for each closing before you choose, and add any transactional funding fee.
Who pays transfer tax and title insurance?
It depends on local custom and the contract. In some places the seller pays transfer tax, in others the buyer, or it is split. In a double close you are on both sides, so check each line of both estimates.
Can every title company do a double close?
No. Some will not close back-to-back transactions, and some end-buyer lenders have rules about how recently the seller bought the property. Ask before you go under contract. This page is not legal or tax advice.

## DSCR Calculator for Rental Property Loans (Free)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/dscr-calculator.html

DSCR calculator.
Debt service coverage ratio for a rental property loan: monthly rent divided by the full payment (principal, interest, taxes, insurance and association dues). It also shows the stricter NOI-based ratio and the largest loan that still meets your target DSCR. DSCR loans are mainly a US product; the ratio itself works anywhere.
The formula
PITIA = principal & interest + property taxes + insurance + association dues
DSCR (lender style) = monthly rent ÷ PITIA
NOI = rent − taxes − insurance − dues − other operating costs
DSCR (NOI-based) = NOI ÷ principal & interest
Maximum loan = the loan whose PITIA equals rent ÷ target DSCR
Worked example
Rent is $2,400 a month. A $260,000 loan at 7.25% over 30 years costs $1,774 in principal and interest. Add $300 of taxes and $120 of insurance and PITIA is $2,194. DSCR is 2400 ÷ 2194 = 1.09.
Questions
What is DSCR in real estate?
The debt service coverage ratio compares a property's rent to its loan payment. A DSCR of 1.25 means the rent is 25% more than the payment. DSCR lenders qualify the property on this ratio instead of the borrower's personal income.
What DSCR do lenders require?
Requirements vary by lender and change with the market. Many DSCR lenders look for at least 1.0 to 1.25, and some offer programs below 1.0 with larger down payments or higher rates. Use the target field to test the number your lender gives you.
Why are there two DSCR numbers?
Most DSCR lenders divide rent by PITIA (principal, interest, taxes, insurance and association dues). Commercial lenders and many investors use net operating income divided by debt service, which also subtracts management, repairs and vacancy. The NOI-based number is stricter and closer to real cash flow.
Does interest-only change DSCR?
Yes. An interest-only payment is smaller, so the ratio is higher. Some lenders qualify interest-only loans on the interest-only payment and others on the fully amortizing one. Try both settings.
How do I keep DSCR visible across deals?
Put rent, taxes, insurance, dues and loan terms on the deal record in your CRM, calculate DSCR as a formula, and block a deal from moving to financing when it is under your lender's minimum.
Related free tools
BRRRR calculator · Rental yield & cap rate calculator · MAO calculator · All free tools
Last updated October 2026. For planning only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Check figures with your lender, accountant or lawyer.

## The Kept-Deal Map: 5 Places Wholesaling Deals Leak
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/kept-deal-map.html

The Kept-Deal Map: find where your deals leak.
Most investors don't have a lead problem, they have a leak problem. Money disappears between the marketing dollar and the kept deal, at five points a CRM can measure if it's set up to. This map names the five leak points, what each looks like, what a system that closes it does, and the free tool to measure it from your own numbers.
Tap Yes or No on each leak point below. Nothing is sent anywhere.
Want the detailed version? Take the 10-point Deal Leak Score and compare answers with your team.
1. Spend
Which campaigns produce kept deals, not just leads?
How the leak looks
Leads are counted by source, but contracts and closings are not tied back to the campaign that paid for them. Cost per lead looks fine while cost per deal is unknown.
What a system that closes it does
Lead source is a required field that carries from lead to contract to closing. A report shows spend, leads, appointments, contracts and closed deals by campaign and market.
Measure it
Cost per deal calculator
2. Answer
How many seller calls go unanswered, and what does that cost?
How the leak looks
Calls to marketing numbers roll to voicemail after hours or when reps are busy, and nobody sees the list. A seller calling several investors usually talks to whoever answers first.
What a system that closes it does
Every missed call to a marketing number creates a callback task on the lead with a due time minutes out, assigned to the next available rep, plus a report of missed calls and time to callback.
Measure it
Missed seller call cost calculator
3. Follow-up
How fast does the team act once a seller is engaged, and does anyone fall through?
How the leak looks
Follow-up lives in reps' heads, phones and sticky notes. Leads with no next task quietly die, and nobody can say how long a new lead waited for a first touch.
What a system that closes it does
No open lead without a next task. Time to first touch and time from contract to first seller call are measured, and stalled leads surface automatically in a shared queue.
Measure it
Salesforce Health Check
4. Offer
Is every offer made from the same disciplined numbers?
How the leak looks
Each rep underwrites differently, in a spreadsheet nobody else sees. Offers go out above the real maximum, and the spread disappears after the contract is signed.
What a system that closes it does
Underwriting sits on the deal record: ARV, repairs, rule percentage and fee as fields, MAO as a formula, and a required review step before an offer goes out.
Measure it
MAO calculator
5. Keep
Does your ROI count only the deals that actually closed?
How the leak looks
Revenue is reported when a contract is signed. Cancelled contracts and reduced fees never come back out of the numbers, so campaigns look more profitable than they are.
What a system that closes it does
Booked revenue and closed revenue are separate fields. ROI by campaign is calculated on kept deals only, and fall-outs are tracked with a reason.
Measure it
The Monday 5
Watch the series
Six short videos, one leak each, with a "steal this" fix you can set up in any CRM. Example numbers are labeled as examples.
1. The 5 leaks
2. Missed seller calls
3. Leads with no next step
4. Offers off-formula
5. Fall-outs in your ROI
6. The Monday 5
All Deal Leak videos, with the free tool for each
Questions
What is Deal Leak?
Deal Leak is the profit a home-buying or wholesaling business loses between paying for a seller lead and keeping a closed deal: the unanswered call, the lead with no next step, the offer made off-formula, and the contract that falls out but still sits in the ROI numbers. It is usually unmeasured, which is why it keeps happening.
What is a kept deal?
A deal that actually closed and paid, at the fee or profit that was actually received. ROI on kept deals leaves out contracts that cancelled or were renegotiated, so it shows what each campaign really returned.
Is speed to lead really that important?
The best-known study (InsideSales.com with MIT's Dr. James Oldroyd, 2007, about 15,000 web leads across six companies, not real estate) found that calling within 5 minutes instead of 30 gave roughly 100x higher odds of making contact and 21x higher odds of qualifying the lead. A Harvard Business Review study (2011) found firms that responded within an hour were about 7x more likely to qualify the lead. No comparable study exists yet for real estate investors.
Do I need Salesforce to close these leaks?
No. Any CRM can close most of them if lead source carries through to closing, every lead has a next task, underwriting lives on the deal, and ROI is calculated on kept deals. Salesforce makes sense when you run several markets, teams or channels and have outgrown simpler investor CRMs.
What does the CRM Revenue Audit do with this map?
The audit (USD 1,500, 10 working days) goes through your CRM and phone data leak point by leak point, sizes each leak from your own numbers, and gives you a prioritized fix list. You can implement it yourself or with me.

## Missed Seller Call Cost Calculator (Speed to Lead)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/missed-call-cost-calculator.html

What do missed seller calls cost you?
Use your own numbers from your phone system and CRM. The calculator turns unanswered calls into lost deals and lost profit, per month and per year. Nothing you type leaves your browser.
An estimate from your inputs, not a promise. Example numbers are made up for illustration.
How the math works
How is the cost of missed seller calls calculated here?
Missed calls = inbound calls × missed %. Lost leads = missed calls × the share of those callers who never get reached. Lost deals = lost leads × lead-to-contract % × contract-to-close %. Lost profit = lost deals × average profit per deal. Every number comes from your inputs.
What is speed to lead?
The time between a seller reaching out (call, form, text) and a real person on your team responding. A seller who is calling several investors usually talks to whoever answers first.
How do I find my missed-call rate?
From your phone system's call log (RingCentral, CallRail, Aircall and similar): inbound calls to marketing numbers that went to voicemail or were abandoned, divided by all inbound calls in the same period.
What does a missed-call alert look like in a CRM?
When a call to a marketing number is missed, the CRM creates a task on the lead with a due time a few minutes out, assigns it to the next available rep, and alerts them. A report then shows missed calls and how long each took to get a callback.

## The Monday 5: KPIs for Real Estate Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/monday-5-real-estate-kpis.html

The Monday 5: five numbers to see before the week starts.
Every Monday an investor team decides where money goes. These five numbers turn those decisions from memory into data. Answer the self-check on each card: every "No" is a decision being made without data.
Cost per appointment, by campaign
Which channel is actually worth the money?
Formula
Campaign spend ÷ appointments set from that campaign's leads.
Look for
Compare channels side by side (mail, PPC, cold calling, texting). Lead volume alone hides the real price.
In Salesforce
Campaign cost on the campaign, appointments counted from lead and opportunity records by source.
Contracts per campaign
Where do signed deals really come from?
Formula
Signed contracts traced back to the original lead source and campaign.
Look for
Channels with fewer leads but more contracts. Make sure repeat sellers keep their first source.
In Salesforce
Source carried from lead to opportunity to transaction, and locked so it can't be changed by accident.
Contract to first seller call
Are we keeping deals warm until closing?
Formula
Hours between “under contract” and the first logged call to the seller.
Look for
Deals where nobody called the seller for days. That's where cancellations start.
In Salesforce
A date stamp at contract, the first logged call after it, and a scorecard by rep.
Booked revenue, forecast vs. actual
What did we book, and how close was the forecast?
Formula
Expected profit when a deal goes under contract, compared with what it actually closed for.
Look for
A gap that grows over time means underwriting or renegotiation needs attention.
In Salesforce
Booked revenue by week and month, plus the original contract price locked at signing.
ROI that counts the deals you keep
Is our best channel being undercounted?
Formula
(Profit from closed deals + value of kept properties − campaign spend) ÷ campaign spend.
Look for
Rentals and deals closed outside the usual flow. Leave them out and your best channel looks average.
In Salesforce
A flag for kept or off-book deals with a profit value, included in campaign ROI.
Questions
What are the most important KPIs for a real estate wholesaling business?
The Monday 5: cost per appointment by campaign, contracts per campaign, time from contract to first seller call, booked revenue forecast vs. actual, and ROI that includes kept deals. Together they show where marketing money works and where deals leak.
Why cost per appointment instead of cost per lead?
Lead counts include wrong numbers, tire-kickers and duplicates. An appointment means a real seller conversation, so cost per appointment is much closer to what a channel actually costs you.
Can I track these without Salesforce?
Yes, in any CRM that keeps lead source on the record from first contact to closing and logs calls with timestamps. The hard part is usually attribution: making sure the source survives from lead to contract to closed deal.
Work out your numbers
Cost per deal by lead source · Missed seller call cost · Glossary

## Moving Off Podio: A Migration Checklist for Wholesalers
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/podio-alternative-wholesalers.html

Moving off Podio: a migration checklist for wholesalers.
Leaving Podio is mostly a data decision, not a software one. Decide what history you keep, carry lead source through to every closed deal, plan for what Podio's Excel export leaves out, and test with 50 records before you move the rest. The checklist below covers it in ten steps.
Signs you've outgrown your current setup
Check the ones that are true
☐ Monday numbers get rebuilt in a spreadsheet by hand ☐ Closed deals don't show which campaign produced them ☐ Missed seller calls don't become callback tasks on their own ☐ The person who built the workspace has left, and nobody wants to touch it ☐ A second market or a bigger team is coming
Two or more checked usually means it's time to rebuild or move. Score the whole funnel in two minutes with the free Deal Leak Score .
Three options
1. Rebuild in Podio
Cheapest when the team knows Podio and the problems are messy fields and missing automations. Rebuild against the wholesaling CRM checklist .
2. Move to an investor CRM
Built for wholesaling and quick to start. Check lead source carried to the closed deal and fall-out reasons before you sign.
3. Move to Salesforce
More setup, but it fits teams with their own process, several markets or custom reporting. I build on Salesforce, so weigh that.
The 10-step migration checklist
1. List every app, field and automation in the workspace
2. Decide what moves: open leads, active deals, buyers, closed deals with source
3. Map each field to the new system; fix picklists and drop unused fields
4. Keep lead source, created date and closed date on every record
5. Export each app (Excel export, filtered batches above 20,000 items)
6. Plan separately for comments, files and tasks (not in the export)
7. Merge duplicate sellers by phone and email
8. Import 50 records, check them with the team, fix the mapping
9. Move the rest, reconnect phone, text and web forms, then cut over
10. Keep Podio read-only for 30 days; compare Monday numbers in both
Export details from Podio's help page on exporting to Excel : an export from the first All items view includes all fields plus created on, created by and tags; images, files, tasks, comments and activity are not included; each export is capped at 20,000 items.
Questions
What does a Podio Excel export include?
Per the Podio help page, an export from the first All items view includes all app fields plus metadata such as created on, created by and tags. Images, files, tasks, comments and activity are not included, and each export is capped at 20,000 items, so larger apps are exported in filtered batches.
How do I keep comments and call notes when I leave Podio?
They are not in the Excel export, so plan for them separately: decide which notes matter (often only open deals and active sellers), and move those through the Podio API or by hand. Archive the rest as a read-only export.
How long does a migration take?
It depends on the number of apps, records and integrations. The slow parts are usually deciding what to keep and cleaning duplicates, not the import itself. Run a 50-record test before the full move.
Should I rebuild in Podio instead?
Sometimes yes. If the team knows Podio and the problems are messy fields and missing automations, a clean rebuild against the checklist can be the cheapest fix.
Can you migrate Podio to Salesforce?
Yes, that is part of my work. I build Salesforce for real estate investors and wholesalers, so weigh my view with that in mind.

## Wholesaling CRM Questions, Answered Plainly | Amr Magdy
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/questions-from-wholesalers.html

Wholesaling CRM questions, answered plainly.
Fifteen questions wholesalers and investors asked in Facebook groups, BiggerPockets and Quora in October 2026, paraphrased with names removed. Each answer is short, practical advice with one concrete step to set up in your CRM, whichever CRM you use, and a link to the free tool or video that goes deeper. Any dollar figure here is an example, not a result.
The questions
Do motivated sellers drop off in the last two or three months of the year?
I'm starting out with a full-time cold caller. What workflow should I set up first?
How do you monitor cold callers’ metrics and calls when they use your dialer account?
Which CRM should I use to build pipelines for my VAs: REsimpli, FreedomSoft, XLeads or something else?
I sent seven contracts last month and none got signed. What am I doing wrong?
My VA makes over 4,500 calls a week and gets no solid leads. What should I check?
What's the most consistent source of motivated seller leads?
How do I calculate my offer price, or maximum allowable offer (MAO)?
How fast should I call back a missed seller call?
How do I know which marketing actually makes money?
I pull pre-foreclosure, probate and driving-for-dollars lists. How do I stop calling the same owner three times?
If my marketing budget went to zero tomorrow, where would my next deal come from?
What is the best CRM for real estate investors?
How much should a real estate investor spend on a CRM?
After a BRRRR refinance, how do you pay back the new loan?
Do motivated sellers drop off in the last two or three months of the year?
Not in a way you should plan around without checking your own numbers. Seller motivation comes from situations like probate, vacancy, divorce, back taxes and repairs the owner can't afford, and those don't stop for the holidays. What often changes is contact: people are busier, travel more and pick up fewer unknown calls. Some investors also pause marketing at year end, which can mean less competition for the sellers who are ready. The honest answer for your market is in your own history, not in a group thread.
Do this in your CRM: Build one report of leads, appointments and signed contracts by month and by lead source, going back at least twelve months. Compare November and December with the rest of the year for each channel, then decide whether to cut, hold or shift spend.
Cost per deal by lead source calculator → The Monday 5 →
I'm starting out with a full-time cold caller. What workflow should I set up first?
Set up the handoff before the dialing. A cold caller's job is to find interested sellers and pass them on cleanly, so the first thing to build is what happens after a yes: which details get captured (address, motivation, timeline, asking price, condition), who gets the lead, and how fast they call back. Then define a short list of call outcomes the caller picks on every call, such as no answer, wrong number, not interested, call back later and interested. Without those, you can't coach the caller and you can't tell a bad list from a bad pitch.
Do this in your CRM: Create a qualified lead stage with those details as required fields, and an automation that assigns each new qualified lead to you with a callback task due the same hour. Make call outcome a required field on every logged call.
Video: Leads with no next step → Wholesaling CRM glossary →
How do you monitor cold callers’ metrics and calls when they use your dialer account?
Give every caller their own login, even on one dialer account. With a shared login, nobody can see who did what. With separate users, each call, recording and outcome is tied to one person, and you can compare callers working the same list. Track a few numbers per caller per day: dials, conversations with a real person, interested leads passed on, and the mix of call outcomes. Then listen to a handful of recordings each week, some picked at random and some marked interested. The numbers tell you where to look; the recordings tell you why.
Do this in your CRM: Sync dialer calls to the lead record with the caller as the owner, and build a daily dashboard grouped by user that shows dials, conversations, leads passed on and outcomes.
The Monday 5 → Salesforce Health Check →
Which CRM should I use to build pipelines for my VAs: REsimpli, FreedomSoft, XLeads or something else?
The brand matters less than whether it does four things for your setup. One: separate logins and permissions, so each VA sees only the leads and stages they work. Two: pipeline stages you name yourself, with required fields before a lead moves forward. Three: your dialer and texting tools log calls and outcomes onto the lead automatically, not by copy and paste. Four: lead source stays on the record from first contact to closed deal, so you can report cost per deal by channel. Test any investor CRM against those four points during a trial, with a VA doing real work in it. Salesforce makes sense once you run several markets, teams or channels.
Do this in your CRM: Before you buy, write your stages on paper (new, contacted, qualified, appointment, offer, contract, closed, dead), rebuild them in the trial, and run five real leads through end to end.
Salesforce for real estate investors → The Kept-Deal Map →
I sent seven contracts last month and none got signed. What am I doing wrong?
Look at the system before the script. Three things usually explain a run of unsigned contracts. First, the offer: if each one is worked out differently, some will be too low for that seller's situation and others too high to work for you. Use one formula and write down the inputs. Second, follow-up: a sent contract with no scheduled next touch goes cold, and a seller talking to several investors often signs with whoever followed up. Third, reasons: if you don't record why each contract wasn't signed (price, timing, family, another buyer, no response), you'll keep guessing. After a month of recorded reasons, the pattern is usually clear.
Do this in your CRM: Add a contract sent stage that requires a follow-up task within 24 hours, and a required “reason not signed” picklist when a deal moves to dead.
MAO calculator → Video: Offers off-formula →
My VA makes over 4,500 calls a week and gets no solid leads. What should I check?
Check four things, in this order. List quality: how old is the list, how was it skip traced, and how many numbers come back wrong or disconnected? If wrong numbers dominate, more dials won't help. Numbers tracked: dials alone say little; you need conversations, interested sellers and appointments to see where the drop happens. Call timing: compare contact rates by hour and day of week, because the hours that work vary by list and market. Call outcomes: if an outcome isn't logged on every call, you can't tell a bad list from a bad pitch. Then listen to a few recorded conversations.
Do this in your CRM: Make call outcome required, tag each lead with its list name and pull date, and run a weekly report of conversations and interested sellers by list and by hour of day.
Cost per deal by lead source calculator → Wholesaling CRM glossary →
What's the most consistent source of motivated seller leads?
The one that produces closed deals at the lowest cost in your market, and the only way to know which one that is, is to measure it. Ask a group and you'll hear cold calling, texting, direct mail, PPC and driving for dollars, and each answer is true for somebody. Comparing sources by cost per lead misleads, because cheap leads often convert worse. Compare cost per signed contract and cost per closed deal by source, over at least a quarter. For example, a channel with expensive leads can still be your cheapest per deal if more of its leads close.
Do this in your CRM: Make lead source a required field that stays on the record from first contact to closing, and report spend, leads, contracts and closed deals by source every month.
Cost per deal by lead source calculator → Video: The 5 leaks →
How do I calculate my offer price, or maximum allowable offer (MAO)?
Start with the common formula: MAO = after-repair value (ARV) × your rule percentage − repairs − your wholesale fee. Many buyers use 70%, but markets often use anything from 65% to 80% depending on price point and competition, so treat it as a dial, not a law. Example only: with an ARV of $200,000 at 70%, repairs of $30,000 and a $10,000 fee, MAO is $140,000 − $30,000 − $10,000 = $100,000. ARV should come from recent sold comps of similar renovated homes nearby, and repairs from a walkthrough plus a contingency. The formula is only as good as those two inputs.
Do this in your CRM: Put ARV, repairs, rule percentage and fee as fields on the deal, calculate MAO with a formula field, and require a review before any offer above MAO goes out.
MAO calculator → Video: Offers off-formula →
How fast should I call back a missed seller call?
As fast as you can: within minutes if possible, and the same hour at the latest. A seller calling from your marketing may be calling other investors too, and usually talks to whoever answers first. The research on speed to lead isn't from real estate, but it points the same way. A Harvard Business Review study (2011) found firms that responded to a lead within an hour were about 7x more likely to qualify it. No comparable study exists yet for real estate investors, so measure your own time to callback and what it costs you.
Do this in your CRM: Have every missed call to a marketing number create a callback task on the lead, due in a few minutes and assigned to the next available rep, plus a daily report of missed calls and time to callback.
Missed seller call cost calculator → Video: Missed seller calls →
How do I know which marketing actually makes money?
Count only the deals you keep. Many reports count revenue when a contract is signed, but cancelled contracts and renegotiated fees never come back out, so some campaigns look profitable when they aren't. Kept-deal ROI compares what a campaign cost with the fees you actually received on deals that actually closed. To get there, lead source has to stay attached from first call to closing, and booked revenue and closed revenue have to be separate numbers. Review it every week with a short list of numbers rather than a crowded dashboard.
Do this in your CRM: Add separate booked fee and closed fee fields on the deal, a required fall-out reason, and a report of spend against closed fees by campaign. Check it every Monday.
The Kept-Deal Map → The Monday 5 →
I pull pre-foreclosure, probate and driving-for-dollars lists. How do I stop calling the same owner three times?
Match on the property, not the person. The same owner often shows up on several lists with slightly different names or mailing addresses, so matching on owner name misses duplicates. Standardize the property address before you import (street suffixes, unit numbers, ZIP) and keep one record per property, with every list it came from attached as a source. Add the filing or pull date as a field so the newest records get called first. That stops three people calling one seller with three different stories, and when one of those leads becomes a deal you can see which list produced it.
Do this in your CRM: Use the standardized property address as the duplicate rule on import, store each list as a related source record, and add a filing date field your call queue sorts by.
Cost per deal by lead source calculator → CRM field kit →
If my marketing budget went to zero tomorrow, where would my next deal come from?
Start with the leads you already paid for. Most investor CRMs hold sellers who said not now and never got a second or third call. Pull every lead from the last 12 to 24 months that never reached a contract, sort by last contact date, and call the oldest first. Some of those situations have changed since: the tenant left, the repairs got worse, the probate settled. Nobody else is calling them because the list is yours. It isn't free, since it costs rep time, but it's usually the cheapest deal flow you have.
Do this in your CRM: Build a list view of leads with no contract and no activity in 90+ days, sorted by last contact date, and give it to one rep as a weekly call block.
Deal Leak Score → Missed seller call cost calculator →
What is the best CRM for real estate investors?
There isn't one best CRM for everyone. Pick the one your team will actually keep updated, and check that it answers three questions: which marketing campaign produced each closed deal (not just each lead), whether every open lead has a next task with a date, and what each closed deal cost by source without exporting to a spreadsheet. Most investor-specific CRMs, such as REsimpli, InvestorFuse and Podio-based setups, can do all three if they're set up that way. Salesforce makes sense once you run several markets, teams or channels and need reporting and automation the simpler tools can't do; it costs more to set up and needs someone to own it.
Do this in your CRM: Before choosing, run five real leads from first call to closed deal in a trial and check you can answer those three questions at the end.
Deal Leak Score → CRM field kit →
How much should a real estate investor spend on a CRM?
Judge it by cost per closed deal, not by the monthly software price. The subscription is usually the smaller cost; the bigger costs are setup time and the deals that slip through when the CRM isn't used. Spend what it takes to get three things working: every lead keeps its marketing source through to closing, every open lead has a next task, and you can see cost per closed deal by source each month. If a cheaper tool does that and your team uses it every day, it's the right one. Move up to something like Salesforce when several markets or teams need reports or automation the simpler tool can't give you.
Do this in your CRM: Measure one month first: leads in, leads followed up within a day, and leads that became contracts. That tells you what problem the CRM has to solve.
Cost per deal by lead source calculator → Acquisitions team capacity calculator →
After a BRRRR refinance, how do you pay back the new loan?
The refinance doesn't make the debt go away, it replaces it, and the rent pays it back. You buy and rehab with cash or a short-term loan. Once the property is rented and appraised at its new value, a long-term lender gives you a new mortgage, often 70% to 80% of the appraised value for an investment property. That loan pays off the short-term loan and returns some or all of your cash. From then on, the rent covers the monthly payment, taxes, insurance and repairs, and what is left is your cash flow. So the test of a good BRRRR is not only whether you got your cash back, but whether the rent still covers the new payment with room to spare.
Do this in your CRM: Keep purchase, rehab, appraisal, new loan and rent as fields on each property, with cash left in the deal and monthly cash flow as formulas, so every refinance is checked the same way.
BRRRR calculator → DSCR calculator →

## Rental Yield & Cap Rate Calculator (USD, CAD, GBP, EUR)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/rental-yield-calculator.html

Rental yield & cap rate calculator.
Gross yield, net yield, cap rate and cash-on-cash return for any rental or buy-to-let property. Include purchase costs such as closing costs, stamp duty or transfer tax as one figure. Built for real estate investors in the United States, Canada, the UK and Europe. Pick your currency; the math is the same everywhere.
The formula
Gross yield = annual rent ÷ purchase price
Net operating income (NOI) = annual rent × (1 − vacancy) − running costs
Net yield = NOI ÷ (price + purchase costs + renovation)
Cap rate = NOI ÷ purchase price
Cash-on-cash = (NOI − annual mortgage payments) ÷ cash invested
Worked example
A $250,000 property with $10,000 of purchase costs rents for $1,750 a month. Gross yield is 8.40%. Allow 5% for vacancy and $4,500 a year of running costs and the net operating income is $15,450, a 5.94% net yield and a 6.18% cap rate. With a $187,500 repayment mortgage at 5.5% over 25 years ($13,817 a year), cash flow is $1,633 a year on $72,500 invested.
Questions
What is the difference between gross and net rental yield?
Gross yield is the annual rent divided by the purchase price, before any costs. Net yield subtracts running costs and vacancy, and divides by everything you paid including purchase costs and renovation. Net yield is the one to compare properties with.
Is cap rate the same as net yield?
Close, but not the same. Cap rate is net operating income divided by the purchase price only. Net yield in this calculator divides by price plus purchase costs and renovation, so it is usually a little lower. US investors tend to quote cap rate; UK and European investors tend to quote yield.
What is a good rental yield?
There is no single number. Yields depend on the country, city, property type and interest rates. Compare a property against similar rentals in the same area, and check that the cash flow is positive after the mortgage.
Should I include stamp duty or transfer tax?
Yes, in purchase costs. Stamp duty in the UK, land transfer tax in Canada, transfer tax in the US and registration or transfer taxes across Europe all add to what you paid, so they lower your net yield. Rates and surcharges for additional properties vary; check the current rules where you buy.
How do I track yield across a portfolio?
Store rent, running costs, purchase costs and loan terms as fields on each property record in your CRM, with yield and cash flow as formulas. A portfolio report then ranks properties by net yield every month.

BRRRR calculator · DSCR calculator · Cost per deal by lead source · All free tools
Last updated October 2026. For planning only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Check figures with your lender, accountant or lawyer.

## Salesforce CRM for Canadian Real Estate Investors

A CRM that tracks every deal — built for Canadian investors.
I'm Amr Magdy. I build the CRM a real estate investment business runs on: every seller lead answered, every offer on record, every deal tracked from first call to close, and ROI counted only on deals that close. I work with Canadian investors, wholesalers and BRRRR investors remotely, on Eastern and Central business hours.
Sound familiar?
Seller calls and web leads go unanswered after hours and nobody calls back.

## Salesforce vs Investor CRMs (Podio, REsimpli and Others)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-vs-investor-crms.html

Salesforce vs investor CRMs: how far each one goes.
Investor CRMs like REsimpli come ready for wholesaling and are the faster start. Podio lets you build your own apps. Salesforce goes furthest on data model, automation, reporting and testing, but costs more and needs to be set up. The right pick depends on your team size, markets and the reports you need.
Side by side
What you need | Salesforce | Podio | Wholesaling CRMs
Built for wholesaling out of the box | No. You build the objects, stages and automations (or hire someone to). | No. You build your own apps. | Yes. Pipeline, stages and seller fields come ready.
Your own data model | Custom objects: 200 on Enterprise, 500 custom fields per object ( source , source ). | Custom apps built from field types, linked with relationship fields ( source ). | Custom fields on the built-in records; check the vendor for custom objects.
Automation | Flow: record-triggered, scheduled, screen and approval flows, built in ( source ). | Podio Workflow Automation, with plan limits on flows and monthly actions ( source ). | Drip sequences and task rules vary by product; ask for a demo of yours.
Reporting | Any field is reportable; joined reports (Enterprise and up) and reporting snapshots for trends ( source , source ). | Ask for a demo of the exact reports you need. | Ask for a demo of the exact reports you need.
Test changes before going live | Sandboxes: copies of your org for testing ( source ). | Not checked. | Not checked.
Calling and texting | Through AppExchange apps and integrations. | Not checked. | Often built in; REsimpli plans differ by calling and SMS minutes ( source ).
Price | Per-user monthly list prices, but most businesses get a discount from a Salesforce account executive based on the business and number of users. Plus setup. | See the vendor's pricing page. | See the vendor's pricing page.
Checked October 20, 2026 against each vendor's own pages. "Not checked" means I could not confirm it from an official page. Products change, so confirm in a demo.
How far Salesforce goes
Your process, not a fixed pipeline
One object for each thing you track: lead, property, offer, contract, buyer and assignment, all linked. Enterprise allows 200 custom objects and 500 custom fields per object, far more than an investor team needs.
Automation without code
Flow runs when a record changes (contract signed, so title and dispo get tasks), on a schedule (every Monday, "not ready" leads come back) and for approvals (an offer over MAO needs a manager). See the automations I'd build first .
Any question as a report
Cost per closed deal by lead source, offers over MAO by rep, days from first call to contract. Joined reports put marketing spend and closed deals in one view; reporting snapshots save the pipeline weekly so you see the trend. See the pipeline dashboard .
Built to grow
Sandboxes to test changes before they go live, field history on up to 20 fields per object ( source ), access by team and market, a daily API allowance that starts at 100,000 requests on Enterprise ( source ), and AppExchange, which lists more than 7,000 apps and consulting partners ( source ).
When Salesforce is overkill
Stay with an investor CRM if
You're solo or a small team doing a few deals a month, and the built-in pipeline fits how you work.
Salesforce makes sense when
You run several teams or markets, you need reports your tool can't build, or your process doesn't fit their pipeline. It should pay for itself in deals you keep, so get a quote first: most businesses are offered a discount on list price.
Questions
Is Salesforce better than an investor CRM?
Not for everyone. An investor CRM is built for wholesaling out of the box and is quicker to start. Salesforce fits when you have several teams or markets, need reports your current tool cannot build, or your process does not fit a fixed pipeline. I build on Salesforce, so weigh my view with that in mind.
How much does Salesforce cost for a small investor team?
Salesforce lists per-user monthly prices on its pricing page, but most businesses don't pay list. Talk to a Salesforce account executive: many teams are offered a discount based on the business and the number of users. Setup is extra, whether you do it yourself or hire someone.
Can Salesforce do what Podio does?
Podio lets you build custom apps from its field types and link apps with relationship fields. Salesforce does the same with custom objects and lookup fields, and adds built-in Flow automation, joined reports, reporting snapshots and sandboxes for testing changes.
Do I need a developer to run Salesforce?
Not for most investor setups. Objects, fields, page layouts, Flow automations and reports are built with point-and-click tools. Code is only needed for unusual integrations or logic.
What is the first step if I want to compare?
Write your stages from new lead to closed on paper, list the five reports you want every Monday, and ask each vendor to show you that exact flow and those reports in a demo.

## Seller Lead Follow-Up Cadence Builder for Investors (Free)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/seller-follow-up-cadence.html

Seller follow-up cadence builder.
Silence is not a no. Pick how hot the lead is, the date you first spoke, and the channels you use. You get a dated touch plan you can follow by hand or import into your CRM as tasks. It is a starting template: adjust it to your market and your own results.
Your touch plan
# | Date | Day | Channel | Purpose
Rules that make any cadence work
Every open lead has a next touch date
A lead with no next task is a lead nobody will call. Make the next touch date required before a rep can save a call outcome.
Stop on a no, not on silence
Silence is not a no. Move a quiet lead to a slower cadence instead of closing it. Close it only when the seller says no, sells, or the property no longer fits, and record the reason.
Log channel and outcome on every touch
After a few hundred touches you can see which channel and which touch number actually gets replies, and replace guesses with your own numbers.
Re-rate the temperature after each conversation
A cold lead whose situation changes (a job move, a vacancy, a repair bill) becomes hot. Changing the temperature should restart the cadence from that date.
Questions
How many times should I follow up with a seller lead?
Until they say no or sell, not until you get tired. The cadence changes with the lead: a seller with a near deadline gets touches every few days, a seller who said "not now" gets a touch every month or quarter. What matters is that every open lead has a next touch date.
Should I call or text first?
Test it on your own list rather than guessing. Split a list in half, call first on one half and text first on the other, and compare reply rates after a few weeks. Log the channel on every touch so you can see the answer.
What is a hot, warm and cold seller lead?
In this builder, hot means a seller with a reason and a timeline under about a month, warm means interested but one to six months out, and cold means not now. Use your own definitions, but write them down so every rep labels leads the same way.
Is texting sellers legal?
Rules on texts and calls to consumers vary by country and US state, and several states are stricter than federal law. Check the rules that apply to you, and consent requirements, before you scale texting. This builder plans touches; it does not send anything.
How do I load the plan into my CRM?
Download the CSV and import it as tasks, or create the same steps as an automated cadence in your CRM. Most CRMs, including Salesforce, can create the next task automatically when the last one is completed.

## Speed to Lead for Real Estate Investors: The First-Hour Rule
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/speed-to-lead-real-estate-investors.html

Speed to lead for real estate investors: the first-hour rule.
Speed to lead is the time between a seller reaching out and a real person on your team talking to them. For investors and wholesalers it decides who gets the deal: motivated sellers usually contact several buyers, and they often go with the first one who answers and sounds able to help. Aim to reach every inbound lead within the hour, and measure it.
What the research says
The best-known study is The Short Life of Online Sales Leads (Harvard Business Review, March 2011) by James Oldroyd, Kristina McElheran and David Elkington. Looking at 1.25 million leads across 42 US companies, firms that contacted a lead within an hour were nearly seven times as likely to qualify it as firms that waited longer, and more than 60 times as likely as firms that waited 24 hours or more. In a separate audit of 2,241 US companies, only 37% responded within an hour and 23% never responded.
That study covered web leads in general, not seller calls. A missed seller call is the same problem in a sharper form: the seller already reached out, and the clock is running against every other investor they called.
How to measure your speed to lead
Lead created time = when the call, form or text came in
First conversation time = when a person on your team actually spoke with the seller
Speed to lead (minutes) = first conversation time − lead created time
Report: median by lead source, by hour of day, and by rep, every Monday
Use the median, because one lead that waited three days will distort an average. Split by hour of day: most teams find their gap is evenings and weekends, which is when many sellers call.
Five rules that fix it in any CRM
1. Every missed call becomes a task
When a call to a marketing number is not answered, the CRM creates the lead if it does not exist and a callback task due in minutes. No missed call should exist only in the phone system.
2. Route to whoever is free
New leads and missed-call tasks go to the next available rep, not to the person who owns the number or the market. A lead waiting for one busy rep is a slow lead.
3. Escalate after 15 minutes
If nobody has touched a new lead or a callback task in 15 minutes, it moves to a second person or a manager. Pick the number that fits your team, then enforce it.
4. Acknowledge after hours, call first thing
Outside business hours, send the seller a short text that a person will call at a set time, then make that call the first task of the morning. Track the acknowledgment and the conversation as separate times.
5. Put the number on the Monday report
Median speed to lead and missed calls not returned, by source. What gets reviewed every week gets faster.
What it costs you
Put your own numbers into the free missed seller call cost calculator : inbound calls, the share you miss, the share you never reach, your conversion rates and average profit. It turns missed calls into lost deals and lost profit per month and per year.
Questions
What is speed to lead?
The time between a seller reaching out (a call, a web form, a text reply) and a real person on your team having a conversation with them. Measure it to the first conversation, not to the first automated text.
What is a good speed to lead for a wholesaler or home-buying company?
Under an hour is the bar the research supports, and in practice the goal is minutes for inbound calls and web forms during business hours. More important than a target is knowing your real number by lead source and by hour of day.
Does an automatic text count as a response?
It helps, because the seller knows they reached someone. But it is not a conversation. Track automated acknowledgment and first human conversation as two separate times.
How do I measure speed to lead if my CRM does not track it?
Add two date-time fields to the lead: when the lead came in and when the first real conversation happened. A formula field gives the minutes between them. Report the median, not the average, by source and by hour.
Why do missed calls matter so much?
A missed inbound call is a seller who already chose to call you. If nobody calls back fast, they talk to the next investor on their list, and the lead never shows up in your CRM at all, so your reports cannot see the loss.

## Wholesale Assignment Fee: Set It So the Deal Still Sells
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/wholesale-assignment-fee.html

Wholesale assignment fee: set it from the buyer's margin.
An assignment fee is what a wholesaler is paid for assigning the purchase contract to a cash buyer. The fee that works is not a round number you pick in advance: it is whatever is left after the buyer's repairs, costs and required profit come out of the after-repair value, minus your contract price. Price it from the buyer's side and deals sell instead of sitting.
The max-fee formula
Buyer's costs = ARV × closing, holding and selling %
Buyer's profit = the profit active buyers in that market need on this kind of deal
Max fee = ARV − repairs − buyer's costs − buyer's profit − your contract price
If max fee is below the fee you need, renegotiate the contract price or pass
Worked example
Made-up numbers to show the math. A house has a $250,000 after-repair value and needs $40,000 of repairs. The buyer's closing, holding and selling costs run about 10% of ARV, so $25,000. Buyers in that area want around 15% of ARV in profit on a medium rehab, so $37,500. Your contract price is $130,000. Max fee = $250,000 − $40,000 − $25,000 − $37,500 − $130,000 = $17,500 . Ask $25,000 and the buyer's profit drops to $30,000; some will pass, and the ones who stay may try to renegotiate before closing.
Run your own numbers in the free wholesale deal analyzer : it shows your MAO, the room under it, the buyer's all-in cost and the buyer's profit and return after your fee.
Assign or double close?
An assignment is usually cheaper: one closing, and the fee is paid at that closing. A double close means you buy the property and resell it, often the same day, so you pay a second set of closing costs and may need transactional funding, but the buyer does not see your spread on the assignment paperwork. Compare the two with your numbers in the assignment vs double close calculator .
What to track in your CRM
Planned fee vs closed fee
Save the fee you expected when you went under contract and the fee that actually closed. The gap shows how often buyers push back and on which kinds of deals.
Fee by lead source and campaign
Average fee per closed deal by source tells you more than lead counts do. A source with fewer leads and bigger fees can beat a cheaper one.
Assignment or double close
A picklist on the deal, plus the extra closing costs on double closes, so the report shows what you actually kept.
Questions
What is an assignment fee?
The amount a wholesaler is paid for assigning their purchase contract with the seller to an end buyer. The buyer pays the seller the contract price and pays the wholesaler the fee, usually at closing.
How much is a typical assignment fee?
There is no standard amount. It depends on the spread between your contract price and what buyers in that market will pay. The useful question is not what is typical but how much fee this deal can carry while the buyer still makes the profit they need.
Does the buyer see my fee?
With an assignment, usually yes: the fee appears in the assignment agreement and on the settlement statement. If a large fee would put the buyer or seller off, a double close is the common alternative, at the cost of a second set of closing costs.
Is assigning a contract legal everywhere?
Rules on wholesaling, assignment and disclosure vary by state and change over time, and some purchase contracts forbid assignment. For example, Oklahoma's SB 1075, in effect since November 1, 2025, requires written disclosures to the seller and a two-business-day right to cancel. This page is not legal advice; check the contract and ask a local real estate attorney before you assign.
What should my CRM track about fees?
The fee on every closed deal, the fee you planned when you went under contract, the lead source and the campaign. That shows which sources produce the deals with the biggest fees and how often fees get cut before closing.
